strengths: Comprehensive and unifying theoretical contribution: The paper establishes a rigorous and complete expressivity landscape for permutation-equivariant weight-space architectures, resolving major open questions regarding their approximation capabilities.

Architectural equivalence theorem: Proves that all prominent permutation-equivariant weight-space architectures (DWS, NP-NFN, HNP-NFN, GMN, NG-GNN) are equally expressive on compact sets, with NFTs matching this class under a mild general-position (GP) assumption. This cleanly unifies what previously appeared to be disparate architectures.

Principled four-tier approximation framework: Distinguishes between function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, and permutation-equivariant operators, providing exact universality boundaries for each.

Deep technical execution: Demonstrates non-universality in full generality via Weisfeiler-Leman indistinguishability and bounded linear regions (for fixed architectures), while establishing positive universality results under natural general-position conditions via continuous canonization and partition-of-unity liftings.

Exceptional presentation and clarity: The main paper provides crystal-clear intuition, illustrative figures, and concise proof sketches, supported by an exceptionally thorough, self-contained 62-page appendix containing complete and rigorous proofs.
weaknesses: Reliance on bias terms for the general-position canonization: The concrete continuous canonization map relies on hidden-layer biases being pairwise distinct ($K \cap \mathcal{E} = \emptyset$). While generic for standard architectures, some architectures omit biases (e.g., standard linear layers with batch/layer normalization or pure linear autoencoders); discussing or sketching extensions to bias-free networks (e.g., using singular values or weight-matrix row norms for canonization) would strengthen the practical relevance.

Exclusion of scale equivariance: The analysis focuses exclusively on the permutation symmetry group $S_{d_1} \times \dots \times S_{d_{L-1}}$, omitting the positive homogeneity / scale symmetries inherent to ReLU networks (e.g., ScaleGMNs), which the authors appropriately acknowledge in limitations but remains an open theoretical frontier.

Lack of empirical corroboration: Although theoretical in scope, simple illustrative synthetic experiments (e.g., showcasing the empirical failure modes on quantized networks where biases collide, or demonstrating the expressivity barrier of fixed-size networks on zoom-out INR operators) would have enriched the paper.

strengths: Unifying and comprehensive theoretical contribution: The paper establishes a complete expressivity landscape for permutation-equivariant weight-space networks, resolving open foundational questions in a rapidly growing area of geometric deep learning.

Architectural equivalence theorem: The proof showing that DWS, NP-NFN (+PE), GMN, and NG-GNN are expressively equivalent (and equivalent to NFTs under general position) elegantly connects disparate model families (message passing, tensor-based equivariant linear layers, transformers) via constructive simulation cycles.

Nuanced and principled four-setting framework: Disentangling function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, and permutation-equivariant operators brings much-needed clarity to the weight-space literature, identifying where prior work conflated distinct approximation regimes.

Sharp characterization of universality boundaries: The paper does not simply prove positive results; it precisely identifies failure modes (e.g., WL-indistinguishable parameter graphs in Proposition 6.2, bounded linear regions for function operators on fixed architectures in Proposition 7.1) and proves universality under natural, mathematically grounded conditions (general position and growing architecture size).
Exemplary rigor and presentation: The manuscript is exceptionally well organized, clearly written, and accompanied by exhaustive, mathematically rigorous proofs in the extensive appendix.
weaknesses: Lack of empirical verification: The paper is purely theoretical. While theoretical analysis is of high standalone value, empirical validation of theoretical insights (such as performance degradation on quantized/degenerate networks in the exclusion set, or scaling behavior for function-space operators) would further strengthen the work.

Reliance on bias terms for canonization: The general position assumption crucially requires distinct bias terms per hidden layer. In certain practical setups (e.g., architectures trained without biases or with heavily regularized/tied biases), canonization via sorting biases is unavailable, meaning universality guarantees in those specific regimes remain open.

strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous theoretical framework: The paper establishes a taxonomy of approximation in weight-space learning by categorizing target maps into four distinct settings (function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, and permutation-equivariant operators). This provides conceptual clarity to a previously fragmented domain.

Unification of prominent architectures: Theorem 5.2 (and Theorem D.6) proves that several major permutation-equivariant architectures (DWS, NP-NFN+PE, GMN, NG-GNN) have equivalent expressive power on compact sets, with NFTs matching this class under general position (Proposition 5.3). This closes important open questions regarding the relative expressive capabilities of message-passing vs. tensor-equivariant architectures on MLPs.

Precise characterization of universality and its failure modes: The manuscript does not merely claim universality; it carefully establishes where universality fails in full generality (due to symmetries and 1-WL graph indistinguishability, e.g., Propositions 6.2 and 7.3) and proves that universality is recovered under mild, Lebesgue-measure-zero general position assumptions (Theorems 6.3 and 7.4).

Insightful analysis of function-space operators: The distinction between fixed-capacity base networks (which fail to approximate complexity-increasing operators like zoom-outs due to bounded linear regions, Theorem F.9) and overparameterized base networks (which achieve universality, Theorem 7.2 / F.10) provides practical design guidance for weight-space model editing and domain adaptation.

Exceptional technical thoroughness: The supplementary material (expanding to over 60 pages) provides complete, mathematically rigorous, layer-by-layer constructive proofs for all equivalences, topological properties of the realization map, and universality theorems.
weaknesses: Restriction to MLPs: The analysis is strictly confined to weight-space networks operating on multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs). While MLPs are standard for initial foundational theory, modern weight-space applications increasingly target convolutional networks, residual blocks, and Transformers, which involve richer and more complex parameter symmetries.

Reliance on the General Position (GP) assumption: The universality results for permutation-invariant functionals and permutation-equivariant operators require pairwise distinct biases per hidden layer. While the authors correctly note that degenerate configurations have Lebesgue measure zero in continuous settings, this assumption fails in low-precision, quantized, or heavily pruned regimes (as acknowledged in Section 6.2).

Lack of empirical validation: The work is purely theoretical. While expressivity theory is independently valuable, empirical validation demonstrating whether existing architectures actually encounter the theoretical expressivity bottlenecks (such as capacity constraints in function-space operators or 1-WL blind spots in practice) would have further strengthened the impact.

Exclusion of scale/sign equivariance: The framework focuses exclusively on permutation symmetries and deliberately sets aside positive scale-equivariance (e.g., ScaleGMNs) and sign-flip symmetries (inherent to activations such as tanh). Extending the unified framework to these additional group actions remains an open challenge.

strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous theoretical foundation: The paper provides the first unified expressivity characterization of permutation-equivariant weight-space networks across four distinct approximation settings (function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, and permutation-equivariant operators).

Expressive equivalence across diverse architectures: Theorem 5.2 establishes that widely used model classes—including DWSNets, HNP-NFNs, NP-NFNs with positional encodings, GMNs, and NG-GNNs—possess identical expressive power, clarifying and unifying the existing architectural landscape.

Sharp characterization of universality and its limits: The manuscript cleanly proves non-universality in full generality using 1-WL indistinguishability counterexamples (Proposition 6.2 and 7.3), and recovers universality under mild, natural general-position (GP) assumptions (Theorems 6.3 and 7.4).

Actionable practical insight: The theoretical insight that fixed-architecture output constraints fundamentally limit function-space operators (Proposition 7.1 and Theorem 7.2) directly motivates the Output Capacity Expansion (OCE) technique, demonstrating substantial empirical gains (up to 34% improvement over prior SOTA on the MNIST INR dilation benchmark without increasing parameter counts).

Exceptional technical depth: The extensive appendix (spanning 71 pages) includes complete, self-contained proofs, an empirical investigation into general-position breakdown under quantization (Appendix G.1), and extensions to transformer weight-space architectures (Appendix H).
weaknesses: Empirical evaluation scope is narrow: The experimental validation is restricted solely to the MNIST INR dilation task. Testing on higher-resolution INRs (e.g., CelebA or CIFAR-10 INRs) or other weight-space tasks such as classifier accuracy prediction or meta-optimization would significantly strengthen the empirical impact.
Missing code repository URL: Footnote 4 on page 9 and Section I state that code, configurations, and logs are available, but the URL is left blank ('Code available at .').

Simplicity of the practical intervention: The proposed Output Capacity Expansion (OCE) simply pools/averages an ensemble of $k$ predicted models. While theoretically motivated by Theorem 7.2, more principled architectures that dynamically expand layer widths or predict deeper/wider output graphs remain unexplored.

strengths: Comprehensive and unifying theoretical framework: The paper resolves a key open question in weight-space learning by demonstrating that prominent architectures (DWS, NP-NFN, HNP-NFN, GMN, NG-GNN) have equivalent expressive power, and that NFTs match this class under general position (GP).

Nuanced taxonomy of approximation settings: The distinction between function-space vs. weight-space targets and functionals vs. operators provides a much-needed, clear framework for analyzing expressivity in neural weight spaces.

Rigorous universality and separation results: The authors provide complete proofs showing when universality holds and when it fails. Notably, they construct concrete counterexamples (e.g., WL-indistinguishable parameter graphs with different ranks) to show where invariant networks fail without GP, and prove universality under natural general-position assumptions via continuous canonization.

Insightful analysis of function-space operators: Proving that fixed-architecture networks cannot approximate operators that increase geometric complexity (e.g., zoom-out/dilation), but that universality is recovered with expanding architecture capacity, addresses a concrete bottleneck in existing literature.

Theory-guided empirical validation: The proposed Output Capacity Expansion (OCE) is directly motivated by Theorem 7.2. When tested on the standard MNIST INR dilation benchmark, it delivers monotonic improvements with ensemble size $k$ while controlling for total parameter count, achieving significant performance gains over prior state-of-the-art methods.
weaknesses: Empirical evaluation is relatively narrow: The experimental verification of OCE is confined to a single benchmark (MNIST INR dilation) on small 3-layer MLPs; evaluating on broader weight-space tasks (such as model accuracy prediction or 3D NeRF editing) would demonstrate even wider practical impact.

Scope of OCE mechanism: While ensembling multiple output networks ($k$-OCE) effectively increases output capacity and verifies the theoretical intuition, it is a relatively basic workaround compared to directly mapping to higher-capacity or differently structured architectures.

strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous theoretical framework: The paper establishes a complete expressivity landscape for permutation-equivariant weight-space networks, categorizing targets into four distinct and practically relevant regimes (function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, and permutation-equivariant operators).

Architectural equivalence theorem: The paper settles an important open question by proving that DWS, NP-NFN, HNP-NFN, GMN, and NG-GNN are expressively equivalent on compact sets, and that NFTs match this class under natural general position (GP) conditions. This unifies a fragmented line of prior literature under a single expressive class.

Sharp characterization of universality and failure modes: The paper identifies clear topological and structural obstructions, demonstrating via 1-WL indistinguishability that invariant networks cannot universally approximate permutation-invariant functionals in full generality, while proving universality holds outside measure-zero exclusion sets via continuous canonization. Furthermore, it cleanly explains why fixed-architecture weight-to-weight maps fail on complexity-increasing function-space operators due to bounded linear regions.

Theory-guided practical solution: Guided by Theorem 7.2, the authors introduce Output Capacity Expansion (OCE), which predicts an ensemble of networks to increase effective output capacity without increasing overall parameter count, achieving up to 34%–46% MSE improvement on the standard MNIST INR dilation benchmark.

Extensive and high-quality mathematical analysis: The appendix is remarkably thorough (71 pages), providing complete proofs for cyclic simulations, topological equivalence of realization spaces, generalization to transformer weight spaces, and empirical analysis of GP breakdown under low-bit quantization.
weaknesses: Limited empirical breadth: The empirical validation of the proposed OCE method is restricted solely to the MNIST INR dilation task. Evaluating OCE or the theoretical takeaways on broader benchmarks (e.g., 3D NeRF/INR editing, neural network property prediction, or meta-optimization) would substantially strengthen the empirical claims.

Focus on expressive capacity without optimization/generalization: The universality and equivalence results concern function approximation in the uniform convergence topology on compact sets, without providing guarantees on trainability with gradient descent or finite-sample generalization bounds (though this limitation is appropriately acknowledged).

Potential degradation in discrete/quantized settings: While the GP assumption holds almost surely for standard continuous float models, the empirical analysis demonstrates that the GP rate collapses rapidly under aggressive quantization (e.g., 8-bit and below), leaving open the design of architectures that maintain universality in heavily discrete/quantized regimes.
